judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 650, which lets the state borrow money to pay for broadband in places that lack it. Montana runs a bonding programme that raises money for building projects. The act adds broadband to the list of things that count as a project, but only where service is poor or missing: areas the state classes as unserved or underserved, and places where the only internet on offer comes by satellite. Broadband is the high-speed internet connection that many rural Montana homes and businesses still lack. Nothing else about how the bonding programme works is changed. The act takes effect on 1 January 2028. The Montana House passed it 61-38, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 665, which protects unpaid officers of small charities from a tax debt. When a company fails to hand over the tax withheld from staff wages, the officer responsible can be made to pay it personally. The act lifts that personal liability for officers and directors of a small nonprofit. Three things bring it back. The protection is lost if the officer is paid for their work, though covering their expenses does not count. It is lost if the charity stays more than 12 months behind with unpaid tax, penalties and interest. And it is lost if the officer takes part in fraud, embezzlement or deliberate wrongdoing. The Montana Senate passed it 36-14, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 104, which lets a state body raise more cheap money for charities and public buildings. The Montana Facility Finance Authority issues bonds so nonprofits and public-benefit facilities can borrow at lower rates. The act triples how much new debt it may take on in any two-year period, from $500 million to $1.5 billion, not counting bonds issued to refinance old ones. From July 2027 that limit rises by a fixed 3% every two years. The act widens which bodies may use the programme to cover 501(c)(3) charities and other public-benefit facilities. The Montana Senate passed it 38-11, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 326, which extends and widens Montana's film tax credits. The credits pay part of the cost of making a film or television programme in the state. They were due to run out, and the act extends them through 2045. It widens which productions and which post-production work can claim. It also pays a bigger credit for hiring veterans and enrolled tribal members. The credit is allocated to certain bodies, and any part they do not use may be claimed by others for a fee. The Montana House passed it 62-38, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 333, which keeps a tax break for coal companies going for two more years. Montana lets a coal producer reduce the severance tax it owes on coal that has been washed. Washing removes rock and other waste before the coal is sold. That break was written to end on 1 July 2025. The act moves the end date to 1 July 2027. Nothing about how the break is worked out changes. The Secretary of State must send a copy of the act to every federally recognised tribal government in Montana. The Montana House passed it 58-42, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 511, which opens up who pays for lawsuits and shuts out money from hostile foreign governments. Sometimes an outside investor pays a person's legal costs and takes a share of any winnings. The act adds rules on what such a funder may do. It bars a government named as an enemy of the United States, and anyone based in or tied to one, from paying for a lawsuit in Montana, directly or through another funder. Other foreign funders may still take part, but the funder must give the Secretary of State their name and a copy of the deal. A party to a case may not pass private business information to any foreign person. The Montana House passed it 77-22, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 534, which frees new internet and mobile phone kit from property tax. Fibre optic cable, coaxial cable and wireless kit first put to use on or after the day the act starts pays no property tax for 5 years. In return the owner must spend the tax saving on new cable or wireless kit in Montana. It has 2 years from the date it first claims the break to do so. Owners must keep records proving it. The act also changes the existing tax cuts for phone and internet property. The Montana House passed it 65-35, and it became law.
